sections.title: Geotechnical Design - Introduction
sections.summary: Allowable bearing capacity is the lesser of the shear failure pressure divided by a factor of safety and the pressure for a specified limiting settlement. The chapter covers bearing capacity theory (5.2), settlement (5.3), sliding resistance (5.4) and global stability (5.5).
sections.body: (p. 47) The design of shallow foundations involves calculating an allowable bearing pressure that will (a) maintain an adequate factor of safety relative to shear failure of the bearing soil, and (b) limit the settlement of the foundation to meet serviceability requirements. The allowable bearing capacity of a shallow foundation is defined as the lesser of: (1) the pressure that will result in a shear failure divided by a suitable factor of safety (FS), or (2) the pressure that results in a specified limiting amount of settlement. This chapter presents the theory behind calculation of allowable bearing capacities, considering both of these important design requirements. It also presents the geotechnical procedures for computing the resistance to sliding for a shallow foundation, and the geotechnical considerations needed to ensure the foundation is stable from a global, or slope stability, perspective.
key_points: Allowable bearing capacity is the LESSER of shear failure pressure / FS and the pressure giving a specified limiting settlement
Both an adequate FS against shear failure and a settlement limit for serviceability are design requirements
Bearing capacity theory: Section 5.2; settlement: 5.3; sliding: 5.4; global (slope) stability: 5.5
sections.applicability: All shallow foundation designs for transportation structures.

sections.title: Allowable Bearing Capacity
sections.summary: Allowable bearing capacity balances shear failure prevention and settlement limitation, both governed by footing width B. For narrow footings, shear failure controls allowable pressure; for wide footings, settlement potential becomes the limiting criterion. Figure 5-1 illustrates this transition conceptually.
sections.body: (pp. 47-48) The allowable bearing capacity of a spread footing historically has combined the design considerations of minimizing the potential for shear failure of the soil and limiting vertical deflection (settlement). Both of these design considerations are a function of the least footing dimension, typically called the 'footing width,' and designated as the variable, B or B_f. In general, for a footing bearing on essentially an isotropic, homogenous material, with no embedment (i.e., founded at the surface), the factor of safety against a shear failure developing beneath the footing will increase as the footing width, B, increases. However, as a footing's dimension increases, the depth of influence also increases. Stated another way, as the footing dimension, B, increases, the stress increase 'felt' by the soil extends more deeply below the bearing elevation. The effect of footing width on bearing capacity and settlement is shown conceptually in Figure 5-1. Note that the allowable bearing capacity of a footing is controlled by shear-failure considerations for narrow footing widths. But as the footing width increases, the allowable bearing capacity is limited by the settlement potential of the soils supporting the footing.
key_points: Allowable bearing capacity combines shear failure prevention and settlement limitation
Both are functions of the least footing dimension, the footing width B (or B_f)
For a surface footing on isotropic, homogeneous material, FS against shear failure increases with B
As B increases the depth of influence also increases: the stress increase reaches deeper below the bearing elevation
Narrow footings: shear failure controls the allowable bearing capacity; wide footings: settlement controls (Figure 5-1)
figures: Figure 5-1: Allowable Bearing Capacity Controlled by Shear Failure Considerations versus Settlement Considerations (conceptual: bearing pressure versus footing width B for FS = 3.0 and for 25-mm (1 in) settlement; shear failure controls narrow footings, settlement wide ones) (p. 48)
sections.applicability: Conceptual framework for all shallow foundation bearing capacity evaluation.

sections.title: Bearing Capacity Theory
sections.summary: Bearing capacity theory defines ultimate bearing capacity as the soil load causing subsurface collapse from shear failure. Settlement results from elastic compression and long-term consolidation. Excessive footing penetration or rotation constitutes failure; this section provides the theoretical basis for preventing it.
sections.body: (pp. 48-49) This section discusses bearing capacity theory and its application toward computing allowable bearing capacities for shallow foundations. Methods of calculating settlement displacements are presented in Section 5.3. When a load is transferred through a footing to the foundation soil/rock, the subsurface materials experience settlement due to elastic (immediate) strains and long-term consolidation (elastic and/or plastic deformation) of the ground. The footing will penetrate into the foundation soil/rock when the intensity of applied loads is such that the load-carrying capacity of the foundation material is exceeded. A foundation failure will occur when the footing penetrates excessively into the ground or experiences excessive rotation (Figure 5-2). Excessive foundation movements such as penetration and rotation of the foundation may cause structural damage or collapse. A failure caused by the vertical and lateral displacement of foundation soils due to lack of sufficient strength is called a 'bearing capacity failure.' The load that develops this type of subsurface collapse is called the 'ultimate bearing capacity' of the soil.
key_points: Ultimate bearing capacity is the load that causes subsurface collapse due to insufficient soil strength
Foundation failure manifests as excessive penetration or rotation
Settlement involves both immediate elastic strains and long-term consolidation
Bearing capacity theory provides the framework for preventing shear failure
figures: Figure 5-2: Bearing Capacity Failure of Silo Foundation (Vesic, 1975, from Tschebotarioff, 1951) (p. 49)
sections.applicability: All shallow foundations where shear failure must be evaluated.

sections.title: Failure Mechanisms
sections.summary: Three modes of bearing capacity failure (Figure 5-4, after Vesic, 1975): general shear (Section 5.2.1.1), local shear (5.2.1.2) and punching shear (5.2.1.3). Soils weak enough to fail in local or punching shear should be avoided for bridge shallow foundations.
sections.body: (p. 49) The printed section has three subsections, one per mode of bearing capacity failure (Figure 5-4, after Vesic, 1975): general shear (Section 5.2.1.1), with well-defined shear planes reaching the surface, footing rotation and bulging on both sides; local shear (5.2.1.2), with failure planes that do not reach the surface and no tilting; and punching shear (5.2.1.3), vertical compression without bulging. Soils so obviously weak as to fail in local or punching shear should be avoided for bridge shallow foundations; Section 5.2.3.6 covers soils in the intermediate, local shear range.
key_points: General shear (5.2.1.1): shear planes extend to the surface, footing rotates, soil bulges on both sides
Local shear (5.2.1.2): failure planes do not reach the surface, bulging but essentially no tilting
Punching shear (5.2.1.3): vertical compression beneath the footing without bulging
Soils weak enough for local or punching shear should be avoided for bridge shallow foundations (see 5.2.3.6)
sections.applicability: Understanding failure modes is essential for selecting appropriate bearing capacity equations and correction factors.

sections.title: General Shear
sections.summary: General shear: a uniform rigid-plastic soil at ultimate bearing capacity develops plastic flow (Prandtl, 1920; Reissner, 1924) with an elastic wedge (Zone I), radial shear on a logarithmic spiral (Zone II) and a passive zone at 45 - phi'/2 (Zone III) (Terzaghi & Peck, 1948). Shear planes reach the surface, the footing rotates and the soil bulges. It prevails in relatively incompressible, reasonably strong soils and in saturated NC clays loaded rapidly (undrained) (Coduto, 1994).
sections.body: (pp. 49-50) The kinematic conditions (strain states) that develop when a uniform, rigid-plastic, weightless soil (cohesion c' and friction phi') reaches the ultimate bearing capacity were determined theoretically by Prandtl (1920) and Reissner (1924): at ultimate load the foundation soils develop plastic flow. Terzaghi and Peck (1948) further defined the zones of plastic equilibrium after failure beneath a continuous footing (Figure 5-3): a triangular wedge beneath the footing, Zone I, remains elastic and moves down with the footing; radial shear develops in Zone II, where radial lines from the footing change length along a logarithmic spiral until the failure plane reaches Zone III; and a passive state develops in Zone III at an angle of 45 - (phi'/2) from the horizontal. This configuration, with well-defined shear planes extending to the surface, footing rotation and bulging of the soil on both sides of the footing, is called 'general shear.' General shear failures (Figure 5-4a) are believed to be the prevailing mode for soils that are relatively incompressible and reasonably strong, or saturated, normally consolidated clays loaded rapidly so that undrained conditions and undrained strength govern (Coduto, 1994).
key_points: Prandtl (1920) and Reissner (1924) derived the strain states of a weightless rigid-plastic soil at ultimate bearing capacity
Zones (Terzaghi & Peck, 1948): I elastic wedge moving down with the footing; II radial shear on a logarithmic spiral; III passive state at 45 - phi'/2 from horizontal
General shear: well-defined shear planes to the surface, footing rotation, bulging on both sides
Prevailing mode for relatively incompressible, reasonably strong soils and for saturated NC clays loaded rapidly (undrained) (Coduto, 1994)
figures: Figure 5-3: Boundaries of Zone of Plastic Equilibrium after Failure of Soil Beneath Continuous Footing (Zones I, II, III) (p. 50)
Figure 5-4: Modes of Bearing Capacity Failure (After Vesic, 1975): (a) General Shear (b) Local Shear (c) Punching Shear (p. 50)
sections.applicability: Recognizing the general shear failure mode that bearing capacity theory describes.

sections.title: Local Shear
sections.summary: Local shear: shear planes are not well developed and do not reach the ground surface; deformation involves vertical compression beneath the footing (Vesic, 1975), bulging at the surface and essentially no tilting. It may occur in relatively loose or soft soils.
sections.body: (p. 51) In some cases the bearing capacity shear planes are not well developed and the failure planes do not extend all the way to the ground surface; this mode (Figure 5-4b) is called 'local shear.' Its deformation involves vertical compression beneath the footing (Vesic, 1975), bulging of the soil at the ground surface and essentially no rotation or tilting of the footing. Local shear failures may occur in soils that are relatively loose or soft compared with soils susceptible to general shear.
key_points: Local shear: shear planes not well developed and not reaching the ground surface
Vertical compression beneath the footing (Vesic, 1975), surface bulging, essentially no rotation or tilting
May occur in soils relatively loose or soft compared with those that fail in general shear
sections.applicability: Recognizing loose or soft soils prone to local shear failure.

sections.title: Punching Shear
sections.summary: Punching shear: vertical compression beneath the footing without bulging, with the load continuing to rise under strain-controlled loading. A potential mode when loose or compressible soils are loaded slowly under drained conditions: deep footings on dense sand, dense sand over soft soil, or soft clay loaded slowly. Soils weak enough for local or punching shear should be avoided for bridge shallow foundations.
sections.body: (p. 51) Another mode under ultimate conditions involves vertical compression of the soils beneath the footing without bulging; as Figure 5-4c shows, the bearing load continuously increases when the footing is loaded under strain-controlled conditions ('test at greater depth'). This is called 'punching shear.' It is a potential failure mode when loose or compressible soils are loaded slowly under drained conditions: footings at great depth on dense sand, or on dense sand underlain by soft, compressible soil, can fail in punching shear, and so can a footing on soft clay loaded slowly. From a bridge foundation design perspective, soils so obviously weak as to experience local or punching shear should be avoided for supporting shallow foundations; Section 5.2.3.6 gives guidance for soils in the intermediate, local shear range.
key_points: Punching shear: vertical compression beneath the footing without bulging; load keeps rising under strain control
Potential mode when loose or compressible soils are loaded slowly under drained conditions
Examples: footings at great depth on dense sand, dense sand over soft compressible soil, soft clay loaded slowly
Soils so obviously weak as to fail in local or punching shear should be avoided for bridge shallow foundations
Intermediate (local shear range) soils: Section 5.2.3.6
sections.applicability: Recognizing punching shear and screening out unsuitable soils for bridge spread footings.

sections.title: Bearing Capacity Equation Formulations
sections.summary: Prandtl/Reissner gross ultimate bearing pressure (Eq. 5-1, factors Eqs. 5-2 to 5-4) plus the N_gamma unit weight term gives Eq. 5-7 for a centrically loaded strip footing; FHWA and AASHTO use Caquot and Kerisel's N_gamma (Eq. 5-8); factors in Table 5-1 and Figure 5-6. Use q_ult gross for the allowable bearing capacity: a net value double-counts the surcharge when structural loads include footing and backfill weight. Scour, excavation and a water table rising to the surface substantially reduce capacity on cohesionless soils.
sections.body: (pp. 51-55) The gross ultimate bearing pressure is the stress the footing applies to the soil at ultimate (failure) conditions at the bearing elevation. Prandtl (1920) and Reissner (1924) developed an expression for it that considers both the frictional and cohesion components of shear strength and a uniform surcharge at the footing base from the embedment depth D_f (Eq. 5-1, with N_q from Eq. 5-2 and N_c from Eqs. 5-3 and 5-4; terminology in Figure 5-5). The net ultimate bearing pressure is the gross value less the surcharge that existed at the bearing depth before the footing was built, q = gamma D_f (Eqs. 5-5 and 5-6); by inspection of Eq. 5-6 the difference is generally small for cohesionless soils (phi > 0). The structural designer will typically include the self-weight of the concrete footing and the backfill over it (approximately gamma D_f) in the applied bearing stress, so a reported net ultimate bearing pressure counts the surcharge over the footing area twice. This is conservative, but generally not recommended, provided that a suitable factor of safety is maintained against bearing capacity failure; if the geotechnical engineer chooses to report an allowable bearing capacity computed from a net ultimate bearing pressure, this should be clearly stated in the foundation report. It is therefore recommended that q_ult gross be used to determine the allowable bearing capacity (q_ult approximately equal to q_ult gross). No analytical solution extends the equations to the unit weight of the foundation material; investigators add an independent term (N_gamma), found by assuming failure surface shapes and running trial analyses, giving Eq. 5-7 for a centrically loaded strip footing. Values of N_gamma proposed by various researchers range from about one-half to double those given here, depending on the friction angle (Chen & McCarron, 1991); FHWA and AASHTO use Caquot and Kerisel's (1948) Eq. 5-8. N_c, N_q and N_gamma versus friction angle are in Table 5-1 and Figure 5-6. By Eq. 5-7 the ultimate bearing capacity depends on c and phi, the effective weight of the soil above and below the footing (gamma or gamma') and the depth and width of the footing (D_f and B_f). For cohesive soils (phi = 0, undrained loading) the last term is zero and the first term is a constant, so the capacity depends only on the cohesion and the embedment depth. Cohesionless soils change greatly in capacity with properties or dimensions, and the embedment effect is particularly important: removing soil over an embedded footing by excavation or scour can substantially reduce bearing capacity and cause footing subsidence, and a rise of the ground water level to the ground surface reduces the effective (buoyant) unit weight, reducing the terms that are a function of unit weight by essentially one-half.
key_points: Eq. 5-1 (Prandtl 1920, Reissner 1924): q_ult gross = c N_c + q N_q, q = gamma D_f; N_q, N_c from Eqs. 5-2 to 5-4 (N_c = 5.14 for phi = 0)
Net ultimate pressure = gross - q (Eqs. 5-5, 5-6); the difference is generally small for cohesionless soils
Recommended: q_ult gross for the allowable bearing capacity; a net value counts the surcharge twice when structural loads include footing and backfill weight
An allowable bearing capacity computed from a net ultimate pressure should be clearly stated as such in the foundation report
Eq. 5-7 adds the unit weight term 0.5 gamma B_f N_gamma for a centrically loaded strip footing
N_gamma = 2(N_q + 1) tan phi (Caquot and Kerisel, 1948), used by FHWA and AASHTO; other authors' values range from about one-half to double
Table 5-1 and Figure 5-6 give N_c, N_q, N_gamma for phi = 0 to 45 degrees
phi = 0 (undrained): capacity depends only on cohesion and embedment depth
Removing cover over an embedded footing by excavation or scour can substantially reduce capacity on cohesionless soils
Ground water rising to the ground surface cuts the unit weight terms by essentially one-half
equations: Eq. 5-1: q_ult gross = c(N_c) + q(N_q); gross ultimate bearing pressure (Prandtl, 1920; Reissner, 1924); c = cohesion of the soil; q = gamma D_f = surcharge at the base of the footing; gamma = unit weight of the overburden material causing the surcharge pressure; D_f = depth of embedment (Figure 5-5); N_q = bearing capacity factor for the surcharge term (p. 51)
Eq. 5-2: N_q = e^(pi tan phi) tan^2(45 deg + phi/2) (p. 51)
Eq. 5-3: N_c = (N_q - 1) cot phi, for phi > 0 deg; bearing capacity factor for the cohesion term (p. 52)
Eq. 5-4: N_c = 2 + pi = 5.14, for phi = 0 deg (p. 52)
Eq. 5-5: q_ult net = q_ult gross - q; net ultimate bearing pressure (p. 52)
Eq. 5-6: q_ult net = c N_c + q(N_q - 1) (p. 52)

Eq. 5-7: q_ult = c(N_c) + q(N_q) + 0.5(gamma)(B_f)(N_gamma); centrically loaded strip footing on a foundation material with unit weight; B_f = footing width; gamma = unit weight of soil beneath the footing; N_gamma = bearing capacity factor for soil unit weight (p. 53)
Eq. 5-8: N_gamma = 2(N_q + 1) tan(phi); Caquot and Kerisel (1948), used by FHWA and AASHTO (p. 53)
figures: Figure 5-5: Design Terminology for Spread Footing Foundation (B_f, L_f, D_f) (p. 52)
Figure 5-6: Bearing Capacity Factors versus Friction Angle (AASHTO, 1996) (p. 55)
sections.applicability: All bearing capacity calculations for shallow foundations. Use Eq 5-7 as the base equation before applying correction factors.

sections.title: Bearing Capacity Correction Factors
sections.summary: Equation 5-7 assumes a rigid strip footing loaded through its centroid on a level surface of homogeneous soil. Semi-empirical correction factors, multiplied into the cohesion (c), unit weight (gamma) and surcharge (q) terms, account for footing shape, ground water, embedment depth, sloping ground, an inclined base, local or punching shear, inclined loading and soil compressibility. Some, but not all, should be used in combination.
sections.body: (p. 55) A number of factors influence the ultimate bearing capacity of shallow foundations that were not included in the derivations discussed earlier. Note that Equation 5-7 assumes a rigid strip (continuous) footing that is loaded through its centroid bearing on a level surface of homogeneous soil. Various correction factors have been proposed by numerous investigators to account for footing shape, location of the ground water table, embedment depth, sloping ground surface, an inclined base, the mode of shear (local or punching shear), inclined loading and soil compressibility. The general philosophy of correcting the ultimate bearing capacity involves using semi-empirical factors that are multiplied by each of the three terms in the bearing capacity equation to account for the particular effect. Each correction factor includes a subscript denoting the term to which the factor should be applied: 'c' for the cohesion term, 'gamma' for the unit weight (footing width) term and 'q' for the surcharge (embedment) term. Each of these factors and suggestions for its application are discussed separately below; in some, but not all, cases the factors should be used in combination, and the following sections say whether certain factors should be combined.
key_points: Correction factors multiply each of the three bearing capacity terms (c, gamma, q) independently
Factors account for: shape, groundwater, embedment depth, sloping ground, inclined base, local/punching shear, inclined loading, soil compressibility
Subscripts c, gamma, q denote which bearing capacity term the factor applies to
Some factors should be used in combination and some should not (e.g., shape with load inclination, Sections 5.2.3.1 and 5.2.3.7)
sections.applicability: All non-ideal footing configurations requiring corrections to the basic strip footing bearing capacity equation.

sections.title: Footing Shape
sections.summary: AASHTO treats a footing with L_f > 5B_f as a strip; correct rectangular footings with L_f/B_f < 5 using Table 5-2. AASHTO (1996) recommends effective dimensions for eccentric loads, but in routine design reasonable assumed footing dimensions are used, since effective dimensions change with load case and the difference is small. Shape factors should not be applied with inclined loading factors.
sections.body: (pp. 55-56) AASHTO guidelines distinguish a strip footing as one whose length (L_f) exceeds five times the footing width (B_f). Corrections of the ultimate bearing capacity should be made for rectangular footings with L_f/B_f ratios less than 5. The shape (eccentricity) correction factors are summarized in Table 5-2. Note that for eccentrically loaded footings, AASHTO (1996) recommends using the effective footing dimensions, B'_f and L'_f, to compute the shape correction factors (refer to Section 6.4.1 for discussion of eccentricity and effective footing dimensions). However, in routine foundation design, this is not practical, since the effective dimensions will change for various load cases, and the difference in the computed shape correction factors will generally be small. Therefore the geotechnical engineer should make reasonable assumptions about the footing shape and dimensions and compute the correction factors using Table 5-2. Note: Shape (eccentricity) factors, s, should not be applied simultaneously with inclined loading factors, i (see Section 5.2.3.7).
key_points: Strip footing: L_f > 5B_f; apply shape corrections when L_f/B_f < 5
Routine design: reasonable assumed footing shape and dimensions, not effective dimensions (see also Section 5.2.4)
Shape (eccentricity) factors should not be applied simultaneously with inclined loading factors (Section 5.2.3.7)
phi = 0: s_c = 1 + B_f/(5L_f), s_gamma = 1.0, s_q = 1.0
phi > 0: s_c = 1 + (B_f/L_f)(N_q/N_c), s_gamma = 1 - 0.4(B_f/L_f), s_q = 1 + (B_f/L_f) tan phi
tables: Table 5-2: Shape Correction Factors (AASHTO 1996): phi = 0: s_c = 1 + B_f/(5L_f), s_gamma = 1.0, s_q = 1.0; phi > 0: s_c = 1 + (B_f/L_f)(N_q/N_c), s_gamma = 1 - 0.4(B_f/L_f), s_q = 1 + (B_f/L_f) tan phi; shape (eccentricity) factors should not be applied simultaneously with inclined loading factors, i (Section 5.2.3.7) (p. 56)
sections.applicability: All rectangular or square footings where L_f/B_f < 5.

sections.title: Location of the Ground Water Table
sections.summary: A water table within the potential zone of shear makes effective stress control the shearing resistance below it. Factors C_W_gamma and C_W_q apply to the two terms with unit weight; the cohesion term is unaffected. Table 5-3: 0.5 and 0.5 with the water at the surface, 0.5 and 1.0 at the footing base, 1.0 and 1.0 below 1.5B_f + D_f; Eqs. 5-9 and 5-10 or interpolation for intermediate depths.
sections.body: (pp. 56-57) If the ground water table is located within the potential zone of shear below or above a footing, effective stresses will control the magnitude of overburden stress and thus the shearing resistance along that portion of the shearing surface that lies below the water table. A simplified method for accounting for the reduction in shearing resistance is to apply factors to the two terms in the bearing capacity equation that include a unit weight term. Recall that the cohesion term is neither a function of soil unit weight nor effective stress. The factors may be computed using the following equations, or by interpolating values between those provided in Table 5-3. C_W_gamma applies to the unit weight (N_gamma) term and C_W_q applies to the surcharge (N_q) term.
key_points: Groundwater correction applies ONLY to terms containing unit weight (N_gamma and N_q terms)
Cohesion term is NOT affected by groundwater position
When water table is at surface (D_W = 0): C_W_gamma = 0.5, C_W_q = 0.5
When water table is at footing base (D_W = D_f): C_W_gamma = 0.5, C_W_q = 1.0
When water table is below zone of influence (D_W > 1.5*B_f + D_f): C_W_gamma = 1.0, C_W_q = 1.0
Interpolate for intermediate positions using Equations 5-9 and 5-10
equations: Eq. 5-9: C_W_gamma = 0.5 + 0.5[D_W / (1.5B_f + D_f)] <= 1.0; ground water correction for the unit weight term; D_W = depth of ground water table (Table 5-3) (p. 56)
Eq. 5-10: C_W_q = 0.5 + 0.5(D_W / D_f) <= 1.0; ground water correction for the surcharge term (p. 56)
tables: Table 5-3: Correction Factor for Location of Ground Water Table (AASHTO, 1998): D_W = 0: C_W_gamma 0.5, C_W_q 0.5; D_W = D_f: 0.5, 1.0; D_W > 1.5B_f + D_f: 1.0, 1.0; for intermediate positions interpolate or use Eqs. 5-9 and 5-10 (p. 57)
sections.applicability: Any footing where groundwater table is within the zone of influence (within 1.5*B_f below or above the footing base).

sections.title: Embedment Depth
sections.summary: Bearing capacity theory treats embedment as a surcharge only and neglects shear through the cover. Where the backfill is high-quality compacted granular material reliably in place over the life of the footing, the depth factor d_q (Table 5-4, 1.15 to 1.40) may be added; otherwise it can be conservatively omitted, and it is 1.0 unless the soils above the bearing elevation are as competent as those below.
sections.body: (p. 57) Because the surcharge term, q, was developed considering the effect on bearing capacity as a vertical pressure applied at the footing bearing elevation, the effect of the shearing resistance as the failure surface passes through the footing embedment cover was neglected in the theory. If the backfill or cover over the footing is known to be of high-quality, compacted granular material that can be reliably assumed to remain in place over the life of the footing, this additional shearing resistance can be included by addition of the embedment depth factor, d_q, shown in Table 5-4. Otherwise, the depth correction factor can be conservatively omitted. Note: The depth correction factor should be used only when the soils above the footing bearing elevation are as competent as the soils beneath the footing level; otherwise, the depth correction factor should be taken as 1.0.
key_points: Depth factor d_q accounts for shearing resistance of embedment cover along the failure surface
Only use when backfill above footing is competent granular material that will remain in place
If soils above bearing elevation are weaker than soils below, set d_q = 1.0
Conservative approach: omit depth correction factor entirely
Values range from 1.15 to 1.40 depending on phi and D_f/B_f ratio
tables: Table 5-4: Depth Correction Factor (Brinch Hansen, 1970): d_q for D_f/B_f = 1, 2, 4, 8: phi = 32 deg 1.20, 1.30, 1.35, 1.40; 37 deg 1.20, 1.25, 1.30, 1.35; 42 deg 1.15, 1.20, 1.25, 1.30; use only when the soils above the bearing elevation are as competent as those beneath, otherwise d_q = 1.0 (p. 57)
sections.applicability: Footings with competent granular backfill above the bearing elevation where embedment effect can be reliably counted.

sections.title: Sloping Ground Surface
sections.summary: Footings on or near slopes need both bearing capacity and overall slope stability checks (Section 5.5). N_cq and N_gamma_q from Figure 5-7 (after Meyerhof, 1957) replace N_c and N_gamma (Eq. 5-11), and the embedment term goes to zero since the surcharge on the slope side is ignored. Beyond a distance b of two to six footing widths the slope has no effect. The cohesionless form is useful for footings in bridge approach fills.
sections.body: (p. 58) Placement of footings on or adjacent to slopes requires that the designer perform calculations to ensure that both the bearing capacity and the overall slope stability are acceptable. The bearing capacity equation should include corrections recommended by AASHTO as adapted from NAVFAC (1986b) to design the footings. Calculation of overall, or global, stability is discussed in Section 5.5. The ultimate bearing capacity equation (Equation 5-7) is therefore modified to include terms N_cq and N_gamma_q that replace the N_c and N_gamma terms (Equation 5-11). Charts are provided (Figure 5-7) to determine these terms for cohesive (phi = 0) and cohesionless (c = 0) soils. Note in Figure 5-7d that beyond a distance, 'b,' of two to six times the foundation width, the bearing capacity is independent of the slope angle (identical to the horizontal ground surface). Also note that the depth of embedment term goes to zero because the surcharge effect on the slope side of the footing should be ignored. Other forms of the equation exist for cohesive soils (phi = 0), but footings on cohesive soils near slopes are likely to be limited by settlement, slope stability or both, so they are omitted; see the NHI Shallow Foundations Workshop Reference Manual (printed 'Munfahk et al., 2000') or NAVFAC DM-7 (1986a, 1986b). The form of the equation that includes the width term on cohesionless soils is useful for designing footings constructed within bridge approach fills. The calculation procedure involves obtaining N_gamma_q from Figure 5-7(c) or 5-7(f) and computing the ultimate bearing capacity using Equation 5-11, or the general form of the bearing capacity expression, Equation 5-14, with the N_gamma term replaced by N_gamma_q.
key_points: For footings on or near slopes, replace N_c with N_cq and N_gamma with N_gamma_q
Beyond 2-6 times footing width from slope edge, bearing capacity equals flat-ground case
Surcharge effect on the slope side of footing should be ignored (embedment term goes to zero)
Must also check overall slope stability (Section 5.5) in addition to bearing capacity
Figure 5-7 gives N_cq (phi = 0, by slope stability factor N_s) and N_gamma_q (c = 0, by phi) for footings on the slope and at a distance b from its edge
Other phi = 0 forms are omitted: such footings are likely limited by settlement or slope stability; see the NHI manual or NAVFAC DM-7
equations: Eq. 5-11: q_ult = c(N_cq) + 0.5(gamma)(B_f)(N_gamma_q); footing on or adjacent to a slope; N_cq and N_gamma_q from Figure 5-7 replace N_c and N_gamma, and the embedment term goes to zero (p. 58)
figures: Figure 5-7: Modified Bearing Capacity Factors for Footing on Sloping Ground (after Meyerhof, 1957, from AASHTO, 1996): (a) geometry, footing on the slope; (b) cohesive soil (phi = 0), N_cq versus slope inclination beta for slope stability factor N_s = 0 to 5; (c) cohesionless soil (c = 0), N_gamma_q versus beta for phi = 30, 40, 45 deg; (d) geometry, footing at distance b from the slope edge; (e) cohesive soil, N_cq versus b/B_f (N_s = 0) or b/H_s (N_s > 0); (f) cohesionless soil, N_gamma_q versus b/B_f; curves for D_f/B_f = 0 and 1, linear interpolation for intermediate depths; N_s = 0 for B_f < H_s, N_s = gamma H_s / c for B_f >= H_s (p. 59)
sections.applicability: Footings located on slopes or within 2-6 footing widths of a slope crest.

sections.title: Inclined Base
sections.summary: Inclined bridge footings should be avoided or limited to inclinations below about 8 to 10 degrees; steeper ones may need keys, dowels or anchors against sliding. Base inclination factors b_c, b_gamma and b_q (Table 5-5, Brinch Hansen, 1970) modify the cohesion, unit weight and surcharge terms.
sections.body: (pp. 58-60) In general, inclined footings for bridges should be avoided, or limited to shallow inclinations, alpha, of less than about 8 to 10 degrees from horizontal. Steeper inclinations may require keys, dowels or anchors to provide sufficient resistance to sliding. If the footing is inclined to the horizontal, the bearing capacity equation should be modified using the factors as determined from Table 5-5. The base inclination factors b_c, b_gamma, and b_q are applied to the cohesion, unit weight, and surcharge terms respectively.
key_points: Avoid inclined footings for bridges; limit inclination alpha to 8-10 degrees from horizontal
Steeper inclinations may require keys, dowels, or anchors for sliding resistance
For phi = 0: b_c = 1 - alpha/147.3, b_gamma = 1.0, b_q = 1.0
For phi > 0: b_gamma = b_q = (1 - 0.017 alpha tan phi)^2 and b_c = b_q - (1 - b_q)/(N_c tan phi)
alpha = footing inclination from horizontal in degrees (upward positive)
tables: Table 5-5: Inclined Base Correction Factor (Brinch Hansen, 1970): phi = 0: b_c = 1 - (alpha/147.3), b_gamma = 1.0, b_q = 1.0; phi > 0: b_c = b_q - (1 - b_q)/(N_c tan phi), b_gamma = b_q = (1 - 0.017 alpha tan phi)^2; phi = friction angle, degrees; alpha = footing inclination from horizontal, upward +, degrees (p. 60)
sections.applicability: Footings with inclined bearing surfaces; rarely used in bridge foundations.

sections.title: Local or Punching Shear
sections.summary: Where local or punching shear can develop (Figure 5-8), AASHTO and others reduce strength to c* = 0.67c and phi* = tan^-1(0.67 tan phi) (Eqs. 5-12, 5-13). At-risk soils (loose sands, sensitive clays, metastable soils, brittle clays) are generally unsuitable for bridge footings anyway. The one-third reduction should NOT be used for NC cohesionless soils in the local shear zone when settlement is checked independently, nor for compacted structural fills of good granular material.
sections.body: (pp. 60-61) Several references, including AASHTO, recommend reducing the soil strength parameters if local or punching shear failure modes can develop; Figure 5-8 shows when they can (a chart for normally consolidated native soil deposits), and the reductions are Eqs. 5-12 and 5-13. Soils that can develop these modes include loose sands, very sensitive clays [S_t > 8; sensitivity is the unconfined compressive strength of an undisturbed sample over that of a remolded sample (Terzaghi & Peck, 1967)], metastable (collapsible, Section 3.1.1) sands and silts, and brittle clays (OCR > 4 to 8; Section 5.3.3). These 'problem' soils should be identified by a thorough geotechnical investigation (Chapter 4); they generally have other characteristics that make them unsuitable for bridge shallow foundations, including large settlement potential for loose sands, sensitive clays and metastable soils. Brittle clays have relatively high strength at small strains but lose much of it at larger strains (strain-softening); this should be identified and quantified by field and laboratory testing and compared with the stress changes from the foundation and ground slope configuration. Local or punching shear can develop in loose sands or under very narrow footings, but seldom applies to bridge foundations, because spread footings are not used on obviously weak soils and relatively large footings are needed for structural stability (Cheney & Chassie, 2000). Two situations where the one-third reduction of Eq. 5-13 can be unnecessarily over-conservative: (1) cohesionless soils falling in the local shear portion of Figure 5-8: a one-third reduction in the tangent of 38 degrees (a common value for good-quality compacted granular fill) reduces N_q by 73 percent and N_gamma by 81 percent, and Figure 5-8 does not consider large footing widths such as those for bridges; provided settlement is checked independently (Section 5.3.4) and found acceptable, spread footings on normally consolidated cohesionless soils in the local shear portion should not be designed with the reduction; (2) footings on compacted structural fill: Figure 5-8 is for normally consolidated natural deposits, and fills compacted to at least 95 percent of maximum density (AASHTO T-180) should have relative density at or above 75 percent (Lee & Singh, 1971), consistent with the excellent performance history of spread footings in structural fills (DiMillio, 1982); the reduction should not be used for footings on compacted structural fills of good-quality granular material. Appendix A has specifications of State highway agencies that routinely build abutment and pier footings in compacted structural fills.
key_points: Eqs. 5-12, 5-13: c* = 0.67c, phi* = tan^-1(0.67 tan phi) where local or punching shear can develop (Figure 5-8)
At-risk soils: loose sands, very sensitive clays (S_t > 8), metastable (collapsible) sands and silts, brittle clays (OCR > 4 to 8)
These problem soils generally have other traits (large settlement potential) that make them unsuitable for bridge shallow foundations
Brittle (strain-softening) clays: quantify by testing and compare with the stress changes from the footing and slope
Seldom applies to bridges: footings are not used on obviously weak soils and are relatively large (Cheney & Chassie, 2000)
A one-third reduction of tan 38 deg cuts N_q by 73% and N_gamma by 81%
No one-third reduction for NC cohesionless soils in the local shear zone of Figure 5-8 if settlement is checked independently (Section 5.3.4) and acceptable
No one-third reduction for compacted structural fills of good granular material: 95% of maximum density (AASHTO T-180) gives D_r >= 75% (Lee & Singh, 1971)
Figure 5-8: B_f* = B_f for square or circular footings; for rectangular footings printed as B_f L_f/2(B_f + L_f)

Eq. 5-13: phi* = tan^-1(0.67 tan phi); reduced friction angle where local or punching shear can develop (p. 60)

sections.applicability: Footings on loose sands, sensitive clays, metastable soils, or other weak/problematic soils where local or punching shear may develop.

sections.title: Inclined Loading
sections.summary: If the axial and shear components of an inclined load are checked against bearing capacity and sliding resistance separately, the load inclination factor can generally be omitted, and GEC-6 omits it from here on; combined with shape factors it is overly conservative. Bearing capacity should use effective footing dimensions where large moments are transmitted, and sliding should be checked for all footings with inclined loads. Unusual column geometry or loading is evaluated case by case.
sections.body: (p. 62) The inclined load case is the resultant formed by both axial and shear load components applied to the footing by the column or wall stem. If the components of this resultant (i.e., axial and shear forces) are checked against the available resistance in the respective direction (i.e., bearing capacity and sliding, respectively), the inclusion of the inclined loading factor in the bearing capacity equation can generally be omitted. The bearing capacity should, however, be evaluated using effective footing dimensions, as discussed in Section 6.4.1 and in the footnote to Table 5-2, since large moments can frequently be transmitted to bridge foundations by the columns or pier walls. The simultaneous application of shape and load inclination factors can result in an overly conservative design. Henceforth, the inclination factor will be omitted in calculation of bearing capacity. A check for sliding stability should be made for all footings with inclined loads. Unusual column geometry or loading configurations should be evaluated case by case against this recommendation to omit the load inclination factors; an example is a strut column not aligned normal to the footing bearing surface, where an inclined footing base may be prudent for bearing efficiency, keeping in mind that bearing surfaces that are not level may be difficult to construct and inspect.
key_points: Inclination factor is OMITTED from bearing capacity calculation per GEC-6 recommendation
Instead, check bearing capacity and sliding resistance separately
Do NOT combine shape factors and inclination factors simultaneously - overly conservative
Use effective footing dimensions for eccentric/inclined loading
Always perform a separate sliding stability check for footings with inclined loads
Unusual column geometry (e.g., a strut column not normal to the bearing surface) is evaluated case by case; an inclined base may be prudent
sections.applicability: All footings with combined vertical and horizontal loading.

sections.title: Soil Compressibility
sections.summary: Vesic's (1975) soil compressibility factors c_q and c_gamma for sands and gravels limit bearing capacity for compression settlement but depend on density and load and ignore layering and the reduction of stress with depth. Because this chapter computes settlement directly, they should not be used for footings on granular soils when a separate settlement calculation is made.
sections.body: (p. 62) Vesic (1975) included correction factors for soil compressibility for footings on sands and gravels, c_q and c_gamma. These factors were developed to effectively limit the allowable bearing capacity accounting for compression settlement of granular materials. The factors are a function of soil density and applied load, and the factors do not account for soil layering or the reduction in stress with depth below a footing. The procedures recommended in this chapter directly compute the estimated compression settlement of footings on sands and granular materials. Therefore, the soil compressibility factors should NOT be used in calculation of ultimate bearing capacity of footings on granular soils when a separate settlement calculation is performed.
key_points: Vesic (1975) compressibility factors c_q and c_gamma should not be used when a separate settlement calculation is performed
The factors were developed to limit allowable bearing capacity for compression settlement of granular materials
They depend on soil density and applied load but ignore soil layering and the reduction in stress with depth (Section 5.3)
This chapter's procedures compute the compression settlement of footings on granular soils directly
sections.applicability: Not recommended for use; perform direct settlement calculation instead.

sections.title: Additional Considerations Regarding Bearing Capacity Correction Factors
sections.summary: The implied FS of a settlement-limited allowable bearing capacity usually makes individual correction factors small. Use full footing dimensions for shape factors; do not combine shape and load inclination factors (Bowles, 1982); applying all factors together can leave 5 percent or less of the uncorrected capacity. Eq. 5-14 is recommended for routine design. A one degree change in friction angle changes the factors 10 to 15 percent, so strength assessment matters more than the corrections.
sections.body:
(pp. 62-63) The inherent or implied factor of safety of a settlement-limited allowable bearing capacity relative to the computed ultimate bearing capacity is usually large enough to render the magnitude of the application of the individual correction factors small. Consider the following observations:

- AASHTO (1996) guidelines recommend calculating the shape, s, factor using the effective footing dimensions, B'_f and L'_f. However, the original references (e.g., Vesic, 1975) do not specifically recommend using the effective dimensions to calculate the shape factor. Since the geotechnical engineer typically does not have knowledge of the loads causing eccentricity, it is recommended that the full footing dimensions be used to calculate the shape factor (Table 5-2) for use in computation of ultimate bearing capacity.

- Bowles (1982) also recommends that the shape and load inclination factors (s and i) should not be combined.

- In certain loading configurations, the simultaneous application of the shape factor correction, the load inclination factor correction, local shear potential, the soil compressibility factors and a suitable factor of safety can result in a computed allowable bearing capacity that is only 5 percent or less of the uncorrected ultimate bearing capacity. This emphasizes the over-conservatism resulting from the simultaneous application of all the factors.

The form of the bearing capacity equation in Equation 5-14 is therefore recommended for routine design applications.

Further, the bearing capacity correction factors were developed assuming that each correction for each of the terms involving N_c, N_gamma and N_q can be found independently. The bearing capacity theory is an idealization. Bearing capacity analysis of foundations is frequently limited by the geotechnical engineer's ability to accurately determine material properties as opposed to inadequacies in the theory used to develop the bearing capacity equations. Consider Table 5-1 and note that a one degree change in friction angle can result in a 10 to 15 percent change in the factors N_c, N_gamma and N_q. Also note that the value of N_gamma more than doubles when the friction angle increases from 35 to 40 degrees. Clearly, the uncertainties in the material properties will control the uncertainty of a bearing capacity computation to a large extent. The importance of application of the correction factors is therefore secondary to adequate assessment through field exploration and laboratory testing of the inherent strength characteristics of the foundation soils.

It should also be noted that very few spread footings of the size used for bridge support have been load tested to failure. The evaluation of bearing capacity is based primarily on theory and laboratory testing of small-scale footings, with modification of the theoretical based on observation.
key_points: Use full footing dimensions (not effective) for shape factor calculation
Do NOT combine shape and inclination factors simultaneously
Simultaneous application of all correction factors can reduce allowable capacity to 5% of uncorrected ultimate - overly conservative
A 1-degree change in friction angle causes 10-15% change in bearing capacity factors
N_gamma more than doubles from phi = 35 to 40 degrees
Accurate determination of soil strength properties is MORE important than precise correction factors
Very few bridge-size spread footings have been load tested to failure; bearing capacity rests mainly on theory and small-scale tests
sections.applicability: Guidance for rational application of correction factors in routine design.

sections.title: Bearing Capacity Calculation
sections.summary: Eq. 5-14 is the general ultimate bearing capacity equation with correction terms for shape (Table 5-2), base inclination (Table 5-5), embedment depth (Table 5-4) and ground water (Table 5-3), recommended for routine design. N_c, N_q and N_gamma come from Table 5-1 or Figure 5-6 (N_cq and N_gamma_q near slopes); friction angles from SPT correlations (Figures 4-1, 4-2) or laboratory or in situ tests.
sections.body: (pp. 63-64) The general form of the ultimate bearing capacity equation including the correction terms is Eq. 5-14, the form recommended for routine design (Section 5.2.4): s_c, s_gamma and s_q are shape factors (Table 5-2); b_c, b_gamma and b_q base inclination factors (Table 5-5); d_q accounts for the shearing resistance along the failure surface through cohesionless material above the bearing elevation (the embedment is otherwise modeled only as a surcharge applied at the bearing elevation; Table 5-4); C_W_gamma and C_W_q are ground water factors (Table 5-3); N_c, N_gamma and N_q come from Table 5-1 or Figure 5-6, and N_c and N_gamma are replaced by N_cq and N_gamma_q for sloping ground or a footing near a slope (Figure 5-7). The friction angle needed for the factors can be correlated from SPT data in cohesionless soil (Figures 4-1 and 4-2) or measured directly by laboratory or in situ tests.
key_points: Eq. 5-14 is the recommended general bearing capacity equation for routine design
Shape s (Table 5-2), base inclination b (Table 5-5), depth d_q (Table 5-4), ground water C_W (Table 5-3) multiply their own terms
N_c, N_q, N_gamma from Table 5-1 or Figure 5-6; N_cq and N_gamma_q replace N_c and N_gamma near slopes
Friction angle from SPT correlations (Figures 4-1, 4-2) or laboratory or in situ tests
equations: Eq. 5-14: q_ult = c N_c s_c b_c + q N_q C_Wq s_q b_q d_q + 0.5 gamma B_f N_gamma C_Wgamma s_gamma b_gamma; general form with correction terms: s = shape (Table 5-2), b = base inclination (Table 5-5), d_q = embedment depth (Table 5-4), C_W = ground water (Table 5-3, Eqs. 5-9, 5-10); N_c and N_gamma become N_cq and N_gamma_q for sloping ground or a footing near a slope (p. 63)
sections.applicability: Primary design equation for all shallow foundation bearing capacity calculations.

sections.title: Bearing Capacity Factors of Safety
sections.summary: Minimum FS against bearing capacity failure for most bridge foundations: 3.0 (typical range 2.5 to 3.5), for unfactored Service Load Design loads. LFD and LRFD factors were calibrated to mimic SLD practice; a resistance factor is not strictly 1/FS. Multiplying allowable capacities by 1.5 to 2 for factored loads should generally be avoided, since the settlement basis used unfactored loads. Mixing SLD capacities with LFD/LRFD loads gives very conservative designs, especially for Load Groups VII-XI.
sections.body: (pp. 64-65) The minimum factor of safety on the calculated ultimate bearing capacity depends on the confidence in the design soil strength parameters (c and phi), the importance of the structure and the consequence of failure. Typical minimum factors of safety for shallow foundations are 2.5 to 3.5; for most bridge foundations a minimum factor of safety of 3.0 against bearing capacity failure is recommended (Cheney & Chassie, 2000). It was selected from applied theory, experience and consensus for comparison with unfactored load combinations [allowable stress, or Service Load Design (SLD)], so the uncertainty in both the loads and the soil bearing strength is combined in this single factor (Eq. 5-15). Load Factor Design (LFD) was first recommended by AASHTO in the late 1970s, with load uncertainty captured in the load factors; only with the AASHTO LRFD Bridge Design Specifications (AASHTO, 1994) was the uncertainty of foundation soil resistances put into performance, or resistance (phi), factors. A resistance factor is not strictly the reciprocal of the factor of safety; it is more properly a partial factor of safety for the potential variation in the computed resistance. The performance (LFD, AASHTO 1996) and resistance (LRFD, AASHTO 1998) factors for shallow foundations were developed by a combination of reliability-based calibration, calibration with SLD (fitting) and engineering judgment, and were selected to match existing practice and mimic allowable stress factors of safety (general LFD equation, Eq. 5-16). Between the adoption of LFD loads and the development of soil resistance factors, agencies using LFD found their designs noticeably more conservative than SLD and made interim provisions, such as multiplying allowable bearing capacities by some factor, say 1.5 to 2; this should generally be avoided, because the settlement computations behind the allowable bearing capacity used unfactored loads, not factored (increased) loads. LRFD (AASHTO, 1994) at least partially resolved these inconsistencies: Appendix C solves two Appendix B examples by LRFD and the designs are not radically different, as expected, since the LRFD resistance factors were selected to give designs similar to past practice. The structural and geotechnical engineers must communicate their design criteria and methods consistently. SLD foundation capacities used with LFD or LRFD load calculations can give very conservative designs, especially for AASHTO SLD Load Groups VII through XI (AASHTO, 1996; Section 6.3), the rare or extreme event loads from earthquake, ice loading and ice plus wind; sizing a shallow foundation for such a group with the geotechnical allowable bearing capacity frequently makes it enormous and impractical, and expensive piles or shafts are then often selected unnecessarily.
key_points: Minimum FS depends on confidence in c and phi, the importance of the structure and the consequence of failure
Typical minimum FS for shallow foundations 2.5 to 3.5; 3.0 recommended against bearing capacity failure for most bridge foundations (Cheney & Chassie, 2000)
FS = 3.0 is for unfactored load combinations (SLD) and combines load and resistance uncertainty (Eq. 5-15)
A resistance factor is not strictly the reciprocal of FS; LFD/LRFD shallow foundation factors were calibrated (reliability, fitting to SLD, judgment) to mimic SLD practice
Multiplying allowable bearing capacities by 1.5 to 2 for LFD loads should generally be avoided: the settlement basis used unfactored loads
SLD capacities with LFD or LRFD loads give very conservative designs, especially for Load Groups VII-XI (earthquake, ice, ice plus wind)
Miscommunication between structural and geotechnical engineers can lead to unnecessary deep foundations
equations: Eq. 5-15: Sum Q_i <= R_n / FS; allowable stress (Service Load Design); Q_i = applied stress (by the spread footing); R_n = yield stress of the member (or ultimate bearing capacity of the soil); FS = the applied factor of safety (p. 64)

Eq. 5-16: gamma Sum beta_i Q_i <= phi R_n; general LFD equation; gamma = load factor for load combination; beta_i = load factor for particular load Q_i; Q_i = particular service load or stress; phi = resistance factor; R_n = nominal strength of member (e.g., yield strength for steel) (p. 64)
sections.applicability: Selection of appropriate factor of safety for all bearing capacity calculations; coordination between structural and geotechnical design methodologies.

sections.title: Presumptive Bearing Capacities
sections.summary: Presumptive bearing capacities: on soil (Section 5.2.7.1) not recommended for final design of transportation structures, only preliminary feasibility and sizing; on rock (Section 5.2.7.2) building code and published allowable pressures for sound rock (Tables 5-6 to 5-8) and Peck et al.'s (1974) RQD correlation (Table 5-9), capped at the rock's unconfined compressive strength and the allowable concrete stress.
sections.body: (p. 65) The printed section is in two parts. Soil (Section 5.2.7.1): presumptive bearing capacities are not recommended for final design of shallow foundations for transportation structures, especially bridges, except for preliminary feasibility and footing sizing. Rock (Section 5.2.7.2): allowable bearing pressures for sound rock from local building codes (Table 5-6, Goodman, 1989), NAVFAC-based presumptive values (Table 5-7) and reduced values for fractured rock (Table 5-8, New York City Building Code, 2001), and the Peck et al. (1974) correlation of allowable bearing pressure with RQD (Table 5-9), which AASHTO recommends, taking the lower of that value and the rock's unconfined compressive strength or the allowable concrete stress.
key_points: Soil (5.2.7.1): presumptive values not for final design of bridges; preliminary feasibility and sizing only
Rock (5.2.7.2): building code values (Table 5-6), NAVFAC-based values (Table 5-7), NYC code for fractured rock (Table 5-8)
Peck et al. (1974) allowable pressure versus RQD (Table 5-9), recommended by AASHTO, not above the rock's unconfined compressive strength or allowable concrete stress
sections.applicability: Preliminary design on soils; final design on rock using presumptive values with engineering judgment.

sections.title: Soil
sections.summary: Presumptive bearing capacities on soil are not recommended for final design of shallow foundations for transportation structures, especially bridges; they are no substitute for site-specific exploration and testing. Exception: preliminary feasibility and footing dimensions for constructability or cost evaluation. Local sources are generally more realistic than values generalized to soil classification or in codes (AASHTO, NAVFAC).
sections.body: (pp. 65-66) The use of presumptive bearing capacities for footings bearing in soils is not recommended for final design of shallow foundations for transportation structures, especially bridges. Guesses about the geology and nature of a site and application of a presumptive value from generalizations in the literature are not a substitute for an adequate site-specific subsurface exploration and laboratory testing program. An exception is preliminary evaluation of shallow foundation feasibility and estimation of footing dimensions for preliminary constructability or cost evaluation. Local sources of suggested presumptive values, available in engineering geology or geotechnical literature, are generally more realistic than capacities generalized to soil classification or found in design codes such as AASHTO (1996, 1998) or the NAVFAC manuals (NAVFAC, 1986a and 1986b).
key_points: Presumptive bearing capacities on soil are not recommended for final design of transportation structures, especially bridges
They are no substitute for site-specific subsurface exploration and laboratory testing
Exception: preliminary feasibility and footing dimensions for constructability or cost evaluation
Local sources are generally more realistic than values generalized to soil classification or found in codes (AASHTO, NAVFAC)
sections.applicability: Preliminary feasibility and sizing of footings on soil; not final design.

sections.title: Rock
sections.summary: Footings on intact sound rock with small loads are generally stable, but investigation must confirm the rock. Presumptive allowable pressures come from building codes (Table 5-6), NAVFAC-based values (Table 5-7, elastic settlement generally under 13 mm), reduced values for fractured rock (NYC code, Table 5-8) and Peck et al.'s RQD correlation (Table 5-9, 29 MPa at RQD 100% to 1 MPa at 0%), which AASHTO recommends but capped at the rock's unconfined compressive strength and the allowable concrete stress.
sections.body: (pp. 66-70) For intact sound rock stronger and less compressible than concrete, footings with small applied loads are generally stable and need no extensive study of rock strength and compressibility, but site investigation is still required to confirm the consistency and extent of the rock beneath the foundation. Allowable bearing capacities for relatively uniform, sound rock are documented in building codes and engineering manuals. 'Sound rock' can generally be defined as a rock mass that does not disintegrate after exposure to air or water, with discontinuities that are unweathered, closed or tight (less than about 3 mm wide) and spaced no closer than 1 m apart. Table 5-6 gives allowable bearing pressures from selected local building codes (Goodman, 1989), developed from experience in sound rock to satisfy both bearing capacity and settlement with a satisfactory factor of safety; following the codes is usually prudent since they tend to be conservative, but for heavy structures presumptive values may lead to overly conservative and costly foundations, and most codes allow a variance supported by an engineering report. Where building codes are unavailable or inapplicable, values such as those in Table 5-7 may be used for sound rock; footings designed with these published values generally have elastic settlements of less than 13 mm. Where rock is reasonably sound but fractured, the Table 5-6 and 5-7 values should be reduced to prevent excessive settlement; most codes give reduced pressures for the degree of fracturing, for example the New York City Building Code (2001), Table 5-8. Peck et al. (1974) correlated presumptive allowable bearing pressure with Rock Quality Designation (RQD), Table 5-9. AASHTO recommends Peck et al.'s values, but if the value exceeds the unconfined compressive strength of the rock or the allowable stress of concrete, the lower of the two should be used. Peck et al.'s values are substantially greater than most other published values and ignore rock type and the condition of discontinuities, but they give a useful upper-bound estimate and a relation between allowable bearing values and the intensity of fracturing and jointing: as RQD drops from 100 to 90 percent, the value falls drastically, from 29 to 19 MPa. RQD is defined as the total sum of pieces of rock core greater than 100 mm (4 in) in length [example: a 1.5-m (60-in) core run with 0.5 m (18 in) of pieces longer than 100 mm gives RQD = 0.5/1.5 = 0.33, or 33 percent]. In no instance should the allowable bearing capacity exceed the allowable stress of the concrete. Peck et al. (1974) also suggested using the average RQD within a depth B_f below the footing base where RQD is relatively uniform there; if rock within 0.5B_f is of poorer quality, its RQD should be used.
key_points: Sound rock: does not disintegrate in air or water; discontinuities unweathered, closed or tight (under about 3 mm) and at least 1 m apart
Site investigation is still required to confirm the consistency and extent of rock beneath the footing
Building code values (Table 5-6, Goodman, 1989) are usually prudent but may be overly conservative for heavy structures; codes allow variance with an engineering report
Table 5-7 (after NAVFAC) where codes do not apply; elastic settlement generally under 13 mm
Reduce Table 5-6/5-7 values for fractured rock; e.g., NYC Building Code (Table 5-8): 5.8, 3.8, 1.9 and 0.8 MPa
Peck et al. (1974), Table 5-9: RQD 100% 29 MPa, 90% 19, 75% 12, 50% 6, 25% 3, 0% 1 MPa (an upper-bound guide)
AASHTO: use Peck et al. values but not above the rock's unconfined compressive strength or the allowable concrete stress
Use the average RQD within B_f below the base; if rock within 0.5B_f is poorer, use the poorer RQD

sections.title: Allowable Bearing Capacities on Soil
sections.summary: Compute the ultimate bearing capacity (Section 5.2.5) and apply an adequate FS (Section 5.2.6), then check settlement under that stress (Sections 5.3.3 to 5.3.5) and reduce the allowable bearing capacity until settlement is tolerable. Soils within about 1.5B below the footing matter most: SPT and sampling at 0.75-m spacing there as a minimum. Bridge footings are frequently governed by settlement, but an adequate margin against shear failure is always kept.
sections.body:
(pp. 70-71) An acceptable and safe design can be achieved by first calculating the ultimate bearing capacity of a spread footing using the procedure in Section 5.2.5 and applying an adequate factor of safety (Section 5.2.6), then performing a settlement analysis to ensure that the foundation will function within performance limits under the applied stress (Sections 5.3.3, 5.3.4 and 5.3.5). If the settlement at the allowable bearing stress is excessive, the allowable bearing capacity must be reduced until the calculated settlement is within tolerable limits. Note that the soils within a zone about 1.5 times the footing width below the footing are the most significant when considering shear failure and settlement. It is therefore beneficial to obtain good data about the subsurface soils in this zone. SPT tests and soil sampling on 0.75-m (2.5-ft) spacing should be considered the minimum level of subsurface data obtained through this zone. Sampling intervals can be reduced to the usual 1.5 m (5-foot) spacing below this level. Borings still must be extended at least through the zone of influence for settlement considerations (two to four times the estimated least footing width), as described in Section 4.3.2.

Remember that allowable bearing capacity also includes consideration for limiting the potential for the footing to settle. The design of shallow foundations for bridges is frequently governed by settlement rather than shear failure considerations, due to the large footing widths. However, an adequate margin of safety should be maintained for all expected loading conditions relative to the potential for shear failure to develop below the footing.
key_points: Step 1: ultimate bearing capacity by Section 5.2.5 with an adequate factor of safety (Section 5.2.6)
Step 2: settlement analysis under the allowable bearing stress (Sections 5.3.3 to 5.3.5)
Step 3: if settlement is excessive, reduce the allowable bearing capacity until it is tolerable
Soils within about 1.5 times the footing width below the footing are the most significant for shear failure and settlement
SPT and sampling at 0.75-m (2.5-ft) spacing through that zone as a minimum; 1.5-m spacing below
Borings must extend through the settlement zone of influence (two to four times the least footing width; Section 4.3.2)
Bridge footings are frequently governed by settlement because of their large widths; keep an adequate margin against shear failure
sections.applicability: Design procedure for determining final allowable bearing capacity on soil.

sections.title: Allowable Bearing Capacities on IGMs and Rock
sections.summary: Confirm IGM and rock properties by site investigation and in situ and laboratory tests, then apply judgment to theoretical bearing capacities combined with local experience (presumptive values). Evaluate whether global stability or rock mass discontinuities limit the allowable capacity; some sedimentary rock loses capacity dramatically with weathering and moisture.
sections.body: (p. 71) The geotechnical engineer should use site investigation, in situ testing and lab testing to confirm material properties of IGMs and rock. Judgment must then be applied to the theoretically computed bearing capacities combined with local experience (presumptive bearing values) when selecting an allowable bearing capacity for design. To preserve stability, the geotechnical engineer must evaluate the potential for global stability or rock mass discontinuities to limit the allowable bearing capacity. Recall that the bearing capacity of some sedimentary rock can dramatically decrease when exposed to weathering and moisture.
key_points: Combine theoretical bearing capacity with local experience and presumptive values for IGMs/rock
Must evaluate global stability and rock mass discontinuities
Sedimentary rock bearing capacity can decrease dramatically with weathering and moisture exposure
Site investigation, in situ testing, and lab testing are essential to confirm material properties
sections.applicability: Design of footings on intermediate geomaterials and rock.

sections.title: Allowable Bearing Capacities on Compacted Structural Fills
sections.summary: Allowable bearing capacity on compacted structural fill depends on fill quality, field compaction and the embankment foundation soils. For sands it can be found rationally from direct shear tests at the proper compaction and stress, but select sand and gravel fills need large equipment, so design combines experience, infrequent lab tests on specified gradations and quality-control specifications. Table 5-10: agency presumptive values 170 to 290 kPa.
sections.body:
(pp. 71-72) Allowable bearing capacities for spread footings constructed on compacted structural fills will be a function of the quality of the fill (e.g., gradation, durability, drainage), the degree of compaction achieved in the field, and the strength and compressibility of the embankment foundation materials. For fill materials such as sands, the design allowable bearing capacity can be determined rationally through laboratory testing such as the direct shear test, conducted at the proper level of compaction and applied stress. The friction angle yielded from such a testing program can be used to directly calculate an allowable bearing capacity.

It is typically desirable and recommended that the compacted structural fills supporting spread footings be a select and specified material that includes sand- and gravel-sized particles. Direct shear testing of such materials requires large test equipment and is therefore not practical on a project-by-project basis. The design of spread footings on compacted sand and gravel materials is therefore a combination of experience and infrequent lab testing on specified gradations of select fill materials. Materials specifications are then developed from the specified gradations to ensure good quality control during construction, which helps keep the lab test conclusions valid for the construction practices used to place the fills.

Table 5-10 lists the presumptive allowable bearing capacities used by some state highway agencies for design of spread footings supported on compacted structural fills. The material and construction specifications associated with these bearing capacities are included in Appendix A.

Direct shear testing at proper compaction and stress level yields friction angle for rational design
Presumptive values (Table 5-10): Washington 290 kPa (3 tsf), Nevada 190 kPa (2 tsf), Michigan 170 kPa (1-3/4 tsf)
Select, specified fill with sand- and gravel-sized particles is desirable; design rests on experience, infrequent lab tests and specifications
Material and construction specifications are in Appendix A

sections.title: Overstress Allowances for Bearing Stresses
sections.summary: Under AASHTO (1996) Service Load Design, certain load groups (e.g., seismic) may exceed the allowable bearing stress by 25 to 50 percent; these overstress allowances for short-duration, infrequent loads may also be applied to calculated allowable bearing capacities.
sections.body: (p. 72) Under Service Load Design (AASHTO, 1996), certain load groups (e.g., seismic) are permitted to exceed the allowable bearing stress of a member (in this case the foundation bearing material) by a specified percentage that ranges from 25 to 50 percent. These overstress allowances are permitted for short-duration, infrequently occurring loads and may also be applied to calculated allowable bearing capacities.
key_points: SLD allows certain load groups (e.g., seismic) 25-50% overstress for short-duration, infrequently occurring loads
The allowances may also be applied to calculated allowable bearing capacities
sections.applicability: Service Load Design checks for extreme or infrequent load combinations.

sections.title: Settlement Estimation
sections.summary: Total settlement combines immediate compression (nearly all of it in cohesionless soils), primary consolidation (cohesive soils) and secondary compression or creep (organic soils, some inorganic silts). Differential settlement, which loads the structure, may frequently matter more than total settlement. Bridges are not exceptionally tolerant of differential settlement, so deformation frequently sets the upper bound of allowable bearing capacity.
sections.body:
(pp. 72-73) The two primary considerations that affect the selection and design of shallow foundations are bearing capacity (discussed in the previous section) and the settlement potential of ground within the zone of influence below the foundation. This section discusses the parameters and methods of analysis used to estimate the magnitude and time-rate of settlement for shallow foundations.

Total settlement of a shallow foundation will result from one, or more likely, a combination of the following:

a) Immediate Compression: This settlement may result from elastic compression of the material supporting the foundation, or from reduction in the pore space in nonsaturated soils due to expulsion of air from the void space. In cohesionless soils, nearly all the settlement that results from an increase in stress is associated with immediate, or elastic, compression.

b) Primary Consolidation: Consolidation settlement occurs when saturated, fine-grained soils experience an increase in stress. The water in the pore spaces initially carries the load. Then, as the water is expelled from the pore space, the soil experiences a reduction in volume and a decrease in the pore space between soil particles. The process can be slow to rapid and is strongly a function of the permeability of the soil in the direction of drainage.

c) Secondary Compression: Some soils, after first experiencing primary consolidation settlement, continue to strain after excess pore-water pressures are dissipated. This process is termed secondary compression, or 'creep.' Organic soils and some inorganic silts are soil types that can exhibit both primary consolidation and secondary compression, or creep, settlement.

Initial compression accounts for the major portion of consolidation in granular soils. Primary compression accounts for the major portion of consolidation in cohesive soils. Primary and secondary compression both contribute significantly to consolidation settlement in organic soils.

Differential settlement occurs when one load-bearing member of a structure experiences total settlement of a different magnitude than an adjacent load-bearing member. Because differential settlement will introduce load and stress in the structure above the foundations, limiting differential settlement may frequently be of more interest in the design of a structure than total settlement. If total settlements are limited, differential settlements will be limited to an even greater extent. Transportation structures, especially bridges, are not exceptionally tolerant of differential settlement, so deformation limitations will frequently form the upper bound of the allowable bearing capacities used to design shallow foundations.
key_points: Three settlement components: immediate compression, primary consolidation, secondary compression (creep)
Granular soils: settlement is primarily immediate/elastic compression
Cohesive soils: settlement is primarily primary consolidation (time-dependent)
Organic soils: both primary and secondary compression are significant
Differential settlement often controls design more than total settlement
Settlement is frequently the governing criterion for bridge shallow foundations
sections.applicability: Framework for all settlement analyses of shallow foundations.

sections.title: Serviceability Criteria
sections.summary: Tolerable movement is expressed as angular distortion delta'/l: below 0.005 for simple spans and 0.004 for continuous spans meets serviceability (Moulton et al., 1982, 1985), about 130 mm over a 30-m continuous span. Bridges are commonly designed for about 25 mm or less (continuous) and 38 to 50 mm (simple spans). DiMillio (1982): 25 to 75 mm caused very little distress in 148 bridges. Rotation, columns within one pier and total sag also need checking.
sections.body:
(pp. 73-74) The tolerable movements a structure can withstand depend on the type of structure, the expected service life and the consequences of excessive movements. Tolerable movements are frequently described in terms of angular distortion between members. 'Angular distortion' is defined as the ratio of the differential settlement (delta') between footings to the span length (l), or delta'/l. The maximum angular distortion should be limited to some acceptable value to minimize structural strength and serviceability problems.

Empirical studies of the performance of bridges subjected to various maximum angular distortions between adjacent foundations concluded that the serviceability criteria would be met if the angular distortion for simple span bridges is less than 0.005 and, for continuous span bridges, less than 0.004 (Moulton et al., 1982, 1985). Using these criteria, a continuous span bridge having a span length of 30 m (100 ft) can tolerate a differential settlement of about 130 mm (5 in) between supports. In practice, bridges are typically designed for tolerable settlements much smaller than this. It is not uncommon for continuous span structures to be designed for differential settlements between adjacent piers of about 25 mm (1 in) or less, and for simply supported spans of about 38 to 50 mm (1.5 to 2 in).

DiMillio (1982) reports in the FHWA research report 'Performance of Highway Abutments on Spread Footings' that moderate differential movements of 25 to 75 mm (1 to 3 in) caused very little distress in any of the structures studied. Of the 148 bridges with spread footings studied, the foundation movements observed were small, and the movements did not cause significant distress.

For large footings on non-uniform soil profiles, or footings with large eccentric loads, footing rotation may be a concern; it can be computed from the potential differential settlement due to the difference in applied loads or the non-uniformity of the soil profile. Tolerable differential movement between adjacent columns within a single pier or bent may be significantly smaller than between adjacent piers, because the superstructure cross beam is rigid and relatively short; the geotechnical and structural engineers should confer when adjacent individual footings under columns of one pier may settle differentially. Total movement may sometimes be the critical criterion: for example, a simply supported single-span structure with predicted settlements of several tenths of a meter at both abutments is not at structural risk from the relatively uniform movement, but the sag in the roadway profile may be unacceptable for ride, safety or aesthetics.
key_points: Angular distortion = differential settlement between footings / span length (delta'/l)
Serviceability met if delta'/l < 0.005 for simple spans and < 0.004 for continuous spans (Moulton et al., 1982, 1985)
A 30-m (100-ft) continuous span could tolerate about 130 mm (5 in); bridges are designed for much less
Common design values: about 25 mm (1 in) or less between piers of continuous spans; 38-50 mm (1.5-2 in) for simple spans
DiMillio (1982): 25-75 mm differential movements caused very little distress; 148 bridges on spread footings studied
Footing rotation may matter for large footings on non-uniform soil or with large eccentric loads
Tolerable movement between columns within a single pier or bent may be much smaller than between piers
Total settlement may govern through roadway sag (ride, safety, aesthetics) even when uniform
