sections.title: Vertical Stress Distribution
sections.summary: Vertical stress increases under uniformly loaded footings come from elastic theory charts (Figures 5-9 to 5-11 for circular, strip and rectangular areas; superposition with Figure 5-11 for irregular or multiple areas), which may be in error by 25 percent or more, or from the simpler, reasonably accurate 2:1 method (Eq. 5-17, Figures 5-12 and 5-13). Other load distributions: Poulos & Davis (1974).
sections.body:
(pp. 74-78) This section discusses methods to determine changes in total vertical stress (delta_sigma_v) due to foundation loading from a spread footing. The following methods for calculating total vertical stress change assume uniformly loaded foundations; other load distributions are in other references (Poulos & Davis, 1974). Methods based on the theory of elasticity are the easiest and most commonly used methods to determine the changes in total stress due to applied foundation pressures. Most closed-form solutions based on the theory of elasticity involve the assumptions that the soil is homogeneous, isotropic and elastic. Lambe and Whitman (1969) report that the stresses predicted under these assumptions agree remarkably well with the relatively few comparisons that have been made to actual measured stresses, but the authors go on to point out that the computed stresses may be in error by as much as 25 percent or more. The charts in Figures 5-9 to 5-11 can be used to estimate the stress increases beneath circular, strip and rectangular loaded areas. The loadings are assumed to be uniform, an assumption found to give reasonable results for settlement prediction.

Note that the principle of superposition may be used with Figure 5-11 to evaluate stresses resulting from irregular or multiple loaded areas. The FHWA EMBANK program (Urzua, 1993) uses these procedures to compute stress increases beneath embankments, for settlement analysis of approach embankments.

Alternatively, stress distributions can also be obtained by assuming a 2-to-1 distribution of stress below the footing, as shown in Figure 5-12. This is much simpler to compute and is a reasonably accurate approximation of the decrease in stress with depth due to an applied surficial load of limited areal extent. A comparison of the simplified 2-to-1 distribution with the actual distributed stress according to elastic theory is shown in Figure 5-13. This distribution can be computed as a function of applied stress according to Equation 5-17.
key_points: Elastic theory methods are standard for computing stress increases beneath footings
Assumptions: homogeneous, isotropic, elastic soil - computed stresses may be in error by 25% or more
Figure 5-9: circular loaded areas; Figure 5-10: strip loads; Figure 5-11: rectangular corner stresses (Newmark chart)
Superposition can be used with Figure 5-11 for irregular or multiple loaded areas
2:1 stress distribution method (Eq 5-17) is simpler and reasonably accurate
FHWA EMBANK (Urzua, 1993) applies these procedures to approach embankments

sections.title: Footings on Cohesive Soils
sections.summary: Settlement of footings on cohesive soils uses one-dimensional consolidation theory, reasonable if FS against bearing failure is at least three; consolidation tests (ASTM D-2435) on undisturbed samples are recommended. Preconsolidated soils can be up to an order of magnitude less compressible; estimating overconsolidation is the principal error. Table 5-11 C_c correlations vary by up to a factor of 5 and are not for final design. Eqs. 5-20 to 5-23 over sublayers typically 1.5 to 3 m thick.
sections.body: (pp. 78-85) Primary and secondary consolidation of saturated clays or clayey deposits may cause substantial settlement; primary consolidation may take weeks to years, and soil properties varying beneath the foundation make its duration and magnitude vary between footings, giving differential settlement. Where a foundation is wide compared with the compressible layer, the soil settles one-dimensionally with very little lateral displacement; from measurements beneath embankments and tanks this is usually reasonable even for narrow foundations provided an adequate factor of safety is applied to bearing capacity (Terzaghi & Peck, 1967), and a desiccated crust or overburden above the footing base limits lateral displacement. Experience suggests one-dimensional estimates are reasonably good as long as the factor of safety is at least three against bearing capacity failure. One-dimensional consolidation testing (ASTM D-2435) on undisturbed samples is recommended for clay compressibility (sampling and load increments: Cheney & Chassie, 2000). Preconsolidated (overconsolidated) soils, compressed in the past by glaciers, since-eroded overburden or desiccation, can be up to an order of magnitude less compressible than normally consolidated soils and can be reloaded below the preconsolidation pressure without large settlement; identifying them by consolidation testing can allow cost-effective shallow foundations. Settlement is estimated from the slope of the void ratio (e) versus log vertical effective stress curve; Figure 5-14 shows the Casagrande (1936) procedure for the preconsolidation pressure sigma'_p, the maximum past pressure (establish a maximum and minimum value and plot the range against depth). The compression index C_c is the slope of virgin compression (stresses above sigma'_p); the recompression index C_R, the slope below sigma'_p, is approximately one-tenth of C_c; e_o is the void ratio at the initial overburden stress. OCR (Eq. 5-18) is 1 for normally consolidated and above 1 for preconsolidated soils, and the expected settlement depends on the loading relative to sigma'_p from corrected consolidation results. Sampling disturbance can mask whether a soil is normally or overconsolidated, so the highest quality samples should be obtained; the principal error in computing settlement of homogeneous clays is in estimating the degree of overconsolidation (Peck et al., 1974), so all available evidence should be used. As a check, c_u/sigma'_v for normally consolidated clays correlates with PI (Eq. 5-19); field values significantly higher suggest overconsolidation, and for a deposit known to be normally consolidated the measured c_u can be checked with it. Settlement is kept to a minimum if the initial effective stress plus the footing stress increase stays below sigma'_p, and where site and economic conditions permit footings may be designed so. The C_c correlations of Table 5-11 can vary by as much as a factor of 5 (using the average trend line) and should not be used for final design of footings on cohesive soils. Primary consolidation of normally consolidated layers (sigma'_p = sigma'_vo) is Eq. 5-20, or Eq. 5-21 when the data are in vertical strain (Figure 5-15); the final stress adds the footing stress change (Section 5.3.2) to the initial effective stress, C_c comes from the corrected consolidation curve of each relevant soil, and the total is the sum over the n layers. A clay below the water table whose water content is closer to the plastic limit than the liquid limit, or whose c_u/sigma'_v exceeds Eq. 5-19, is likely overconsolidated: loading follows the recompression curve up to sigma'_p and the virgin curve beyond, by Eq. 5-22 (Figure 5-16a) or Eq. 5-23 (Figure 5-16b). Each compressible layer within the zone of influence Z_I is subdivided into sublayers, typically 1.5 to 3 m thick in highway bridge work, so that the stresses at their centers are representative and properties reasonably constant; profiles mixing normally and preconsolidated soils use the appropriate combination of Eqs. 5-20 to 5-23.

sections.title: Time Rate of Consolidation
sections.summary: Footings are designed for the settlement that ultimately occurs, so the consolidation rate matters less for them than for approach embankments on soft clay, especially when surcharged to allow a spread footing. Time-rate procedures are beyond GEC-6's scope; embankment and surcharge design is in the Soils and Foundations Workshop Reference Manual (Cheney & Chassie, 2000), and Appendix B Example 3 shows the procedure's elements.
sections.body: (p. 85) Consolidation occurs when a saturated compressible layer of soil is loaded and water is squeezed out of the layer. The time required for the (primary) consolidation process to end will depend on both the compressibility and the permeability of the soil. The rate of consolidation is usually of lesser concern for foundations because superstructure damage will occur once the differential settlements become excessive. Shallow foundations are designed to withstand the settlement that will ultimately occur during the life of the structure, regardless of the time it takes for the settlement to occur. It is generally much more important to predict the time rate of the settlement of an approach embankment on soft clay, particularly if the embankment is surcharged in order to allow use of a spread footing. The procedure for computing the time-rate of settlement is beyond the scope of this document. Design of approach embankments and surcharges for embankment settlement is in the Soils and Foundations Workshop Reference Manual (Cheney & Chassie, 2000); those procedures can manage approach embankment settlement to allow a spread footing in the approach fill, and Example 3 in Appendix B shows the elements of this procedure.
key_points: Time rate depends on both compressibility and permeability of the soil
For foundations, total settlement magnitude is typically more important than time rate
Time rate is more critical for approach embankment settlement management and surcharging
Time-rate procedures are beyond GEC-6; see Cheney & Chassie (2000) and Appendix B Example 3
sections.applicability: Understanding when time-rate analysis is needed versus when total settlement magnitude is sufficient.

sections.title: Secondary Compression
sections.summary: Soils susceptible to secondary compression (creep) are generally too poor to support a shallow foundation: even if primary consolidation is managed by surcharging, the magnitude of secondary compression is too uncertain to found a spread footing on or over them.
sections.body: (p. 85) Soils susceptible to secondary compression (creep) are generally too poor to consider supporting a shallow foundation on them. Even if the primary consolidation can be managed with surcharging, the uncertainty associated with predicting the magnitude of secondary compression settlements is generally too great to reliably found a spread footing on or over creep-susceptible soils.
key_points: Creep-susceptible soils are generally too poor to support shallow foundations
Even with primary consolidation managed by surcharging, secondary compression is too uncertain to predict reliably
Organic soils and some inorganic silts can show both primary consolidation and creep (Section 5.3)
sections.applicability: Screening criterion to avoid shallow foundations on creep-susceptible soils.

sections.title: Footings on Cohesionless Soils
sections.summary: Footings on cohesionless soils are often settlement-controlled; semi-empirical SPT/CPT methods predominate. The Hough method is recommended as the primary tool: conservative and consistent, overpredicting by about 2 (Gifford et al., 1987) or 1.8 (five FHWA load tests). The D'Appolonia method is the most statistically accurate but underpredicted by about 0.77 in the load tests; it and Briaud's PMT load-settlement method are alternates or for more accurate estimates. A locally proven method may be used.
sections.body: (pp. 86-89) Shallow foundations on cohesionless soils (sand, gravel and non-plastic silt), in situ or as engineered fill, are often controlled by settlement rather than bearing capacity, so the settlement method should be reliable (predicted settlement rarely less than observed) yet reasonably accurate so designs are not inefficient. Elastic methods can be unreliable because the modulus of granular soils is hard to measure (true undisturbed sampling is neither simple nor practical, and in situ estimates vary), so semi-empirical methods correlated to large databases of SPT and CPT tests predominate. Two major studies (Burland & Burbidge, 1984; Gifford et al., 1987) included 76 independent case histories relevant to highway bridge footings. Gifford et al. compiled 21 case histories to compare 11 methods, and monitored 21 bridge foundations on spread footings for 3 years from construction to completion; their final study evaluated Burland & Burbidge (1984), D'Appolonia et al. (1968), Hough (1959), Peck & Bazaraa (1969), Schmertmann (1970) and Oweis (1979), plotting measured against calculated settlement 'for each of the five settlement prediction methods' (Figure 5-17, which shows five). In the 1990s FHWA load tested five square footings, 1 m by 1 m to 3 m by 3 m, at the National Geotechnical Experimental Site on the Texas A&M Riverside Campus, characterized by SPT, CPT, PMT, dilatometer, triaxial, borehole shear and other tests (Briaud & Gibbens, 1994, 1995; Briaud et al., 2000); 31 authors submitted alpha predictions of the load for 25 mm (1 in) of settlement, but the methods were applied too variably for valid conclusions on their reliability. The most promising result is a pressuremeter-based load-settlement method (Section 5.3.4.3), of interest for deformation-based analysis, extreme loads such as earthquake, and LRFD (Appendix C). Criteria for a settlement method: reliable over a wide range of soils; no large standard deviation of predicted versus actual settlement (a large one risks large underprediction); easy to implement with readily available, inexpensive site-specific data; and a substantial history of satisfactory use. No method meets all of these outstandingly, but some meet most reasonably well; the Hough and D'Appolonia methods were selected as the currently preferred procedures, with Briaud's load-settlement curve method presented as promising for sands when PMT data are available. In Gifford's data the Hough method overpredicts by a factor of about 2 on average (less than desirable accuracy) but is conservative and consistent, with a relatively low standard deviation (s_o = 0.82); it is SPT-based, easy and inexpensive, already used by many highway agencies with a vast history, and accounts rationally for the stress increase below a footing and for layering. The D'Appolonia method was the most statistically accurate, with the lowest standard deviation (s_o = 0.51); it uses a modulus of compressibility correlated to SPT and explicitly accounts for preloading (on a limited database). Its drawbacks: limited application history for highway bridges; no explicit soil layering; an empirical stress-distribution correction with no limiting depth of influence; a limited database for the modulus correlation; and, being statistically 'accurate', about half the data fall on the unconservative side. The author compared both methods with the five load tests (not a true alpha prediction): Hough overpredicted by an average factor of about 1.8 (s_o = 0.53) and never underpredicted; D'Appolonia underpredicted by an average factor of about 0.77, with generally better accuracy and less scatter (s_o = 0.22), corroborating the earlier studies. Recommendation: the Hough method as the primary design and analysis tool; the D'Appolonia or load-settlement methods as alternates, or when a more accurate estimate is desired, recognizing their shorter history for highway bridges; and if another method is locally or regionally known to be more reliable and meets the criteria, use the best method available.
key_points: Footings on cohesionless soils are often controlled by settlement, not bearing capacity
Semi-empirical SPT/CPT methods predominate; elastic methods suffer from the hard-to-measure modulus of granular soils
Preferred: Hough (primary design and analysis tool) and D'Appolonia; Briaud's PMT load-settlement curve method is promising
Gifford et al. (1987): Hough overpredicts by about 2 on average, s_o = 0.82; D'Appolonia most accurate, s_o = 0.51
Five FHWA load tests: Hough overpredicted by about 1.8 (s_o = 0.53), never underpredicted; D'Appolonia underpredicted by about 0.77 (s_o = 0.22)
D'Appolonia drawbacks: little bridge history, no layering, no limiting depth of stress, limited modulus database, about half of predictions unconservative
Method criteria: reliable, low scatter, easy and inexpensive inputs, substantial history of satisfactory use
A locally proven method meeting the criteria may be used instead

sections.title: Hough Method
sections.summary: Hough (1959) method, for normally consolidated cohesionless soils only: correct SPT N for overburden by Liao & Whitman (1986) (N'/N = 1/(sigma'_vo/95.76)^0.5, sigma'_vo in kPa, 2.0 max., Figure 5-18), read C' from Figure 5-19, split the profile into about 3-m layers to about 3B, compute sigma'_vo and the stress increase at each midpoint, settle each layer by Eq. 5-24 and sum.
sections.body: (pp. 89-90) Hough (1959) developed an empirical method for settlement of shallow foundations on cohesionless soils that follows the approach used for consolidation settlement of clay layers; it applies only to normally consolidated cohesionless soils. Cheney and Chassie (2000) recommend correcting SPT blowcounts for overburden pressure before correlating them to the bearing capacity index C', and recommended the Bazaraa (1967) correction. Since then the 1996 and 1998 NCEER consensus (Youd et al., 2001) concluded that the Liao & Whitman (1986) correction (Figure 5-18) could be used for routine engineering, and it is included here because it is easy to calculate without charts: N'/N = 1/(sigma'_vo/95.76)^0.5, sigma'_vo in kPa, 2.0 maximum. The soil is divided into layers and the effective vertical stress change at mid-height from the applied load is estimated by elastic theory. Steps: (1) correct SPT blowcounts for overburden stress (Figure 5-18); (2) determine C' from Figure 5-19 using the corrected N'; (3) subdivide the profile into approximately 3-m (10-ft) layers by stratigraphy to a depth of about three times the footing width; (4) calculate sigma'_vo at the midpoint of each layer and the layer's average C'; (5) calculate the stress increase at each midpoint, Delta sigma_v, from Figure 5-9, 5-10 or 5-11 or the 2:1 method (Figure 5-12); (6) calculate each layer's settlement Delta H by Eq. 5-24; (7) sum the incremental settlements for the total.
key_points: Applicable only to normally consolidated cohesionless soils
SPT N corrected for overburden by Liao & Whitman (1986), per the NCEER consensus (Youd et al., 2001); Cheney & Chassie (2000) had used Bazaraa (1967)
N'/N = 1/(sigma'_vo/95.76)^0.5, sigma'_vo in kPa, maximum 2.0 (Figure 5-18)
C' from Figure 5-19 by corrected N' and soil type (six curves, clean uniform medium sand to inorganic silt)
Layers about 3 m (10 ft) thick by stratigraphy to about three footing widths
Stress increase at layer midpoints by Figures 5-9 to 5-11 or the 2:1 method; layer settlement by Eq. 5-24, summed
equations: Eq. 5-24: Delta H = H_o (1/C') log[(sigma'_vo + Delta sigma_vf) / sigma'_vo]; Hough method settlement of each layer; H_o = layer thickness; C' = bearing capacity index (Figure 5-19); sigma'_vo = effective vertical stress at the layer midpoint; Delta sigma_vf = stress increase at the midpoint (printed with subscript v f; Step 5 calls it Delta sigma_v) (p. 90)

sections.applicability: Primary recommended method for settlement estimation on normally consolidated cohesionless soils.

sections.title: D'Appolonia Method
sections.summary: The D'Appolonia method computes settlement of sand or sand and gravel by Eq. 5-25 from the applied stress, footing width, correction factors for embedment (mu_o) and sand layer thickness (mu_1) (Figure 5-20) and the modulus of compressibility M correlated with the average SPT in depth B below the footing, separately for preloaded and for normally loaded sand (Figure 5-21). Accuracy and drawbacks: Section 5.3.4.
sections.body: (pp. 90-93) The D'Appolonia method computes settlement in sand or sand and gravel by Eq. 5-25 from the applied stress beneath the footing, the footing width, correction factors for embedment (mu_o) and for the thickness of the sand layer (mu_1) from Figure 5-20 (Christian & Carrier, 1978), and the modulus of compressibility M of the sand from Figure 5-21, correlated with the average measured SPT resistance in depth B below the footing, with separate lines for preloaded sand and for normally loaded sand or sand and gravel; any consistent set of units may be used. Its accuracy and drawbacks are discussed in Section 5.3.4. Other methods, Schmertmann (1970), Peck & Bazaraa (1969) and Terzaghi & Peck (1967), are discussed in the NHI Shallow Foundations Reference Manual (Munfakh et al., 2000).
key_points: Delta H = (Delta sigma_v B_f / M) mu_o mu_1 (Eq. 5-25), any consistent units
M from Figure 5-21 by the average measured SPT in depth B below the footing
Separate M lines for preloaded sand and for normally loaded sand or sand and gravel
mu_o = embedment correction (D/B), mu_1 = sand layer thickness correction (H/B, by L/B) from Figure 5-20
Most statistically accurate in Gifford's study (s_o = 0.51) but potentially unconservative; limited bridge history (Section 5.3.4)
Schmertmann, Peck & Bazaraa and Terzaghi & Peck methods: NHI manual (Munfakh et al., 2000)

Figure 5-21: Modulus of Compressibility (D'Appolonia, 1968, 1970): M versus average measured SPT resistance in depth B below footing (blows/foot), lines for preloaded sand and for normally loaded sand or sand and gravel; data from loading foundations on clean sand or sand and gravel ('Table' = seven case histories including six bridge footings, D'Appolonia et al., 1970; 'Site' = a large steel mill site in northern Indiana, D'Appolonia et al., 1968) (p. 92)
sections.applicability: Alternate method for settlement on cohesionless soils, especially when preloading history is known.

sections.title: Load-Settlement Curve Method
sections.summary: Briaud's pressuremeter method transforms the average PMT curve point by point into the footing load-settlement curve: strain compatibility rho/B = (1/4.2)(Delta R/R_0) (Eq. 5-26), footing pressure from the gamma function (Eq. 5-28, 22 load tests, mean minus one standard deviation) times influence factors for shape, eccentricity, inclination and slope (Eqs. 5-27 to 5-35). Promising, especially for deformation-based design, but new and to be used in parallel with existing methods.
sections.body: (pp. 93-95) Briaud and colleagues (Briaud & Gibbens, 1994, 1995; Briaud et al., 2000) developed a procedure to estimate settlement of spread footings on sand from pressuremeter test (PMT) data, after observing that soil movement below footings in large-scale load tests resembles soil movement around an expanding pressuremeter probe. Procedure: (1) perform pre-bored pressuremeter tests within the footing's depth of influence, typically at 0.5B, 1B and 2B below the bearing elevation (test and data reduction: Briaud, 1989, 1992); (2) reduce the data and average the curves into a single pressuremeter curve; (3) transform it point by point into the footing load-settlement curve with Eqs. 5-26 to 5-35. Eq. 5-26 ensures strain compatibility: the footing limit pressure is at a settlement of 10 percent of the footing width (rho/B = 0.1) and the pressuremeter limit pressure at a relative cavity radius increase of 0.42, which Eq. 5-26 makes correspond. Eq. 5-27 transforms the pressuremeter pressure into footing pressure through the gamma function (Eq. 5-28), developed from 22 footing load tests at 9 sand and silt sites for a square footing loaded vertically at its center on flat ground and taken as the mean minus one standard deviation (conservative), and through influence factors for shape, eccentricity, load inclination and an adjacent slope (Eqs. 5-29 to 5-35), developed from numerical simulations because too few load tests exist for those cases and compared with the few applicable load tests and other recommendations. The method shows significant promise for predicting settlement over a fairly large range of loads and may prove uniquely useful in deformation-based design (not covered here) for extreme loads such as earthquake. Considerations: (1) its developers acknowledge that it is new and needs parallel use with existing approaches on full-scale bridge projects, with performance measurements, before it is a validated everyday design tool; (2) pressuremeter tests are used infrequently compared with the SPT, so the skills to run and interpret them may be locally limited; (3) results in normalized displacement (rho/B) must be reduced to displacement versus footing width for a tolerable settlement to be used in this GEC's design procedures (Chapter 6, Appendices B and C).

Strain compatibility: rho/B = (1/4.2)*(delta_R/R_0) ensures PMT and footing deformations correspond
Gamma function: Gamma = 0.9/[100*(rho/B) + 0.5] + 0.8 (conservative, mean minus one std dev)
Influence factors for shape (f_L/B), eccentricity (f_e), load inclination (f_delta), and slope (f_beta,d)
Influence factors come from numerical simulations (too few load tests for those cases)

Pressuremeter testing is infrequent and the skills may be locally limited
Results in rho/B must be converted to displacement versus footing width for design

Eq. 5-35: f_beta,d = 0.7(1 + d/B)^0.15, beta = 26.6 degrees (2:1 slope) (p. 95)

sections.title: Footings on Structural Fills
sections.summary: Settlement within compacted structural fill can be estimated with the cohesionless soil methods using a representative SPT value: without other data, assume a corrected N' of 32 blows/ft (Gifford et al., 1987), about 85 percent relative density at 100 kPa and 95 percent or more relative compaction (modified Proctor assumed), with the Hough method.
sections.body: (pp. 95-96) Settlement within a structural fill under a footing supported in it requires an assumption about the compressibility of the fill; because structural fills should be good-quality granular material, the methods of Section 5.3.4 apply, given a representative SPT N-value of the compacted fill. Gifford et al. (1987) used a corrected (for overburden pressure) N-value of 32 blows per foot, corresponding to a relative density of about 85 percent at an overburden stress of about 100 kPa (1 tsf) (Figure 4-1); correlations of relative density with relative compaction put this at or above 95 percent relative compaction (Lee & Singh, 1971), approximating most highway agencies' structural fill criteria. Lee & Singh do not state the Proctor test, but the comparisons were for granular soils and mention the modified Proctor method, so modified Proctor is assumed. Without other SPT data in structural fills, the settlement of a footing on structural fill can be estimated with an assumed corrected N-value (N') of 32 and the Hough method.
key_points: Structural fills are good-quality granular material, so the cohesionless soil methods (Section 5.3.4) apply
Gifford et al. (1987): corrected N' = 32 blows/ft as representative of structural fill
N' = 32 corresponds to D_R about 85% at about 100 kPa (1 tsf), at or above 95% relative compaction (Lee & Singh, 1971; modified Proctor assumed)
Without other SPT data: assume N' = 32 and use the Hough method

sections.title: Footings on IGMs and Rock
sections.summary: IGMs are assumed stiff and strong enough that settlement generally does not govern. When needed, estimate rock settlement by elastic theory (Eq. 5-36) with shape and rigidity factor C_d (Table 5-12), Poisson's ratio (Table 5-13, 13 rock types) and intact modulus E_IR (Table 5-14, 16 rock types) reduced by alpha_E = 0.0231 RQD - 1.32 >= 0.15 (Eq. 5-37). The modulus estimate is the main limitation; in situ tests or published values by rock type can supply it.
sections.body: (pp. 96-98) This GEC assumes (Section 3.1.3) that intermediate geomaterials (IGMs) are stiff and strong enough that bearing capacity and settlement will generally not govern a spread footing on them. If a settlement estimate is needed on IGM or rock, a method based on elasticity theory will generally be best, limited mainly by the engineer's ability to estimate the modulus. Eq. 5-36 computes settlement on rock from Young's modulus of the intact rock, with the stress at the top of rock from the methods of Figures 5-9 to 5-12, C_d from Table 5-12, Poisson's ratio from Table 5-13, E_IR from Table 5-14 and the RQD-based modulus reduction factor of Eq. 5-37. Corrections for complex geology, such as layered and anisotropic rock, are in the NHI Shallow Foundations Workshop Reference Manual (Munfakh et al., 2000). The elastic modulus of IGMs and some rocks may be measured in situ with the pressuremeter, the flat dilatometer, plate load tests or flat jacks (The Pressuremeter Test for Highway Applications, FHWA-IP-89-008; The Flat Dilatometer Test, FHWA-SA-91-044; or the relevant ASTM method); values by rock type are available from Bieniawski (1984, 1989), Kulhawy (1975) and Lama and Vutukuri (1978). Tables 5-13 and 5-14 give suggested Poisson's ratio and elastic modulus values as presented in AASHTO (1996), modified after Kulhawy (1978).

sections.title: Sliding and Lateral Stability
sections.summary: Lateral load is resisted by base shear and passive pressure, but passive resistance needs much larger movement and is conservatively ignored. Sliding resistance is (W + P_v) tan delta on frictional soil (Eq. 5-38; tan delta = tan phi for concrete cast on granular soil, else Table 5-15) or c_a B_f on clay (Eq. 5-39, c_a typically c_u), never combined. Minimum FS against sliding 1.5 (Eq. 5-40). A key adds resistance in stiff OC clays and soft rock (Eq. 5-41).
sections.body:
(pp. 99-101) A shallow foundation will resist lateral loads by a combination of the shear resistance along the base of the footing and the lateral earth pressure that develops in front of the footing in the direction of loading. The shear resistance along the base will develop its full capacity at very small deflections. The lateral earth pressure is termed 'passive resistance' and requires much larger deflections to develop the full passive capacity. By the time the passive resistance is fully developed, the shearing resistance is fully mobilized and may even by reduced to some residual value less than the peak shearing resistance. For this reason, the design of most shallow foundations conservatively ignores passive resistance.

Sliding resistance between the base of a shallow foundation and a granular soil will be governed by the coefficient of friction (tan delta) that develops between the foundation soil and the footing. The value of the coefficient of friction is a function of the soil type and the roughness of the footing. For concrete cast against cohesionless or granular material, the coefficient of friction, tan delta, will be equal to the tangent of the friction angle (tan phi) for the soil supporting the footing. If the bottom of the footing consists of something other than concrete cast against the ground, then the coefficient of friction (tan delta) is not solely a property of the soil but is also a function of the footing material type and roughness. In the absence of specific data, Table 5-15 may be used to estimate the coefficient of friction between soil and various footing material types.

If the base of the footing rests on clay, the sliding resistance will be limited by the adhesion, c_a, that develops between the bearing surface of the footing and the cohesive bearing material. In practice, c_a is typically taken as equal to the undrained shear strength (cohesion, c_u) of the clay.

The general equation for sliding resistance for footings with planar bearing surfaces on frictional (drained) materials is Equation 5-38. For cohesive (undrained) materials, the sliding resistance is given by Equation 5-39. Because drained and undrained conditions will not occur simultaneously, Equations 5-38 and 5-39 should not be combined for use at the same time.

A minimum factor of safety (FS) of 1.5 against sliding should be used for design of bridge foundations (Equation 5-40).

If sliding resistance as determined by Equation 5-39 for a footing on clay soils is insufficient, the footing width should be increased. If impractical, consideration may be given to including a key constructed under the bearing surface of the footing. The general equation for sliding resistance of footings on cohesive soils provided with a key is given by Equation 5-41. Keys are typically difficult to construct while maintaining the intact shearing resistance of the soil adjacent to the key. In reality, keys constructed in granular soils are not very efficient in developing passive pressures; a key in granular soils is more properly considered as increasing the effective length of the shearing surface. In stiff, overconsolidated clays and soft rock, the additional resistance of a key can be computed with Figure 5-22 and Eq. 5-41.
key_points: Passive earth pressure resistance is conservatively IGNORED in most shallow foundation designs
Sliding resistance on granular soil: F_R = (W + P_v) * tan(delta), where delta = friction angle at interface
For concrete cast against granular soil: tan(delta) = tan(phi) of the soil
Sliding resistance on clay: F_R = c_a * B_f, where c_a ~ c_u (undrained shear strength)
Minimum FS against sliding = 1.5 for bridge foundations
Do NOT combine drained (Eq 5-38) and undrained (Eq 5-39) sliding resistance

sections.title: Global Stability
sections.summary: Evaluate global stability when the ground geometry away from the footing makes the bearing capacity theory assumptions invalid and the footing stress acts to destabilize the slope (Figure 5-23). Check it by limit equilibrium, e.g., the method of slices (Bishop, 1955; Spencer, 1967). Detailed guidance: Cheney & Chassie (2000) and TRB Special Report 247 (TRB, 1996).
sections.body:
(pp. 101-102) Global stability of shallow foundations should be evaluated when the geometry of the ground surface in any direction away from the footing suggests that the assumptions associated with the bearing capacity theory used to calculate the bearing capacity of the footing are not valid, and the stress applied by the footing loads is acting to destabilize the slope geometry. Figure 5-23 depicts slope configurations and footing locations that act to either improve or degrade the global stability of the slope.

In cases where the stress applied by the footing acts to destabilize the slope, the global stability of the footing should be checked using limit equilibrium methods such as the method of slices (Bishop, 1955; or Spencer, 1967).

Detailed guidance for the evaluation of slope stability is not included in this Circular. The Soils and Foundation Workshop Reference Manual (Cheney & Chassie, 2000) includes fundamental discussion of slope stability analysis methods considering the presence of a loaded footing within the slope. The reference work TRB Special Report 247: Landslides, Investigation and Mitigation (TRB, 1996) includes more detailed discussion on the analysis of global slope stability.
key_points: Evaluate global stability when the ground geometry invalidates the bearing capacity assumptions and the footing stress acts to destabilize the slope
Footing location can improve or degrade slope stability (Figure 5-23)
Check by limit equilibrium, e.g., method of slices (Bishop, 1955; Spencer, 1967)
Detailed guidance: Soils and Foundations Workshop Reference Manual (Cheney & Chassie, 2000) and TRB Special Report 247 (1996)
Footings on or near slopes need both bearing capacity and overall stability checks (Section 5.2.3.4)
